name: Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID)

summary.text: The Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID) ran a USAID-funded advisory project in Russia in the 1990s, working with Anatoly Chubais's State Property Committee (GKI) on privatization and, under later agreements, on developing a Russian capital market and a legal reform program. Harvard economist Andrei Shleifer directed the project and Jonathan Hay ran its Moscow office. In 1997 USAID suspended and then cancelled the remaining grant, alleging conflicts of interest. In September 2000 the Justice Department sued Harvard, Shleifer and Hay; in June 2004 a federal judge found that Harvard had breached its USAID cooperative agreements and found Shleifer and Hay liable on conspiracy and fraud counts; the case settled in 2005 with Harvard paying $26.5 million, Shleifer $2 million and Hay up to $2 million, none admitting liability. HIID was dismantled in 2000.

facts.claim: USAID contracted with Harvard to direct and manage its economic-reform advisory program in Russia, run out of HIID; the initial award was $2.1 million and the U.S. government ultimately allocated $57 million to the project.
facts.quote: AID, learning that Sachs and Shleifer were in Moscow, contracted with Harvard to direct and manage the reform program. The agency initially gave $2.1 million to Harvard, which would run the operation out of its Harvard Institute for International Development. [...] The U.S. government allocated $57 million for the project, but in 1997, AID pulled the plug, charging Shleifer and Hay with conflict-of-interest violations.

facts.claim: In November 1996 the General Accounting Office reviewed, at congressional request, how USAID awarded assistance agreements to HIID for work in Russia and Ukraine, and HIID's role in implementing agreements to develop a Russian capital market and devise a legal reform program.
facts.quote: Pursuant to a congressional request, GAO reviewed the Harvard Institute for International Development's (HIID) work, focusing on: (1) how the U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) awarded assistance agreements to HIID to carry out work in Russia and Ukraine; and (2) HIID's role and accomplishments in implementing assistance agreements to develop a Russian capital market and devise a legal reform program.

facts.claim: A 1995 GAO report on USAID projects in Russia recorded that consultants from HIID, a USAID contractor, worked with the Russian State Property Committee (GKI) to design and monitor a USAID-supported project.
facts.quote: consultants from another USAID contractor, the Harvard Institute for International Development, worked with GKI to design and monitor the project

sources.title: GAO Report to Congressional Requesters on USAID projects in Russia (NSIAD-95-156)

facts.claim: In the Harvard project's early years Shleifer was assigned to work with Chubais on privatization, while Jeffrey Sachs advised Yegor Gaidar on macroeconomics; Hay set up HIID's Moscow operations inside Chubais's GKI.
facts.quote: Shleifer was assigned to work with Chubais on privatization, while Sachs advised Gaidar on macroeconomics. [...] Jonathan Hay had negligible practical experience, but soon, with Shleifer's blessing, he was setting up Harvard's Moscow operations at Chubais's GKI in a drafty government building near Red Square.

facts.claim: In May 1997 USAID suspended a $14 million grant to HIID pending an investigation into whether two leading figures of its Russia program had used their positions for private profit; on June 6, 1997 USAID cancelled the grant and said it would end all Harvard-run economic-reform programs in Russia by year's end. USAID alleged that Hay had invested in Russian government bonds in violation of its conflict-of-interest rules and that Shleifer's wife had made similar investments using Harvard resources and U.S.-paid staff. Both men denied wrongdoing through their lawyers, and HIID dismissed them from the Russia programs.
facts.quote: USAID suspended a $14-million grant to HIID, pending the conclusion of an investigation into whether two leading figures in the institute's Russia program abused the public trust by using their positions for private profit. On June 6 USAID canceled the grant and said it would terminate all its Harvard-run economic-reform programs in Russia by year's end. [...] Through their lawyers, both Shleifer and Hay denied wrongdoing. HIID dismissed Hay and Shleifer from their work on the Russia programs.

facts.claim: In September 2000 the U.S. Department of Justice sued Harvard University, one tenured professor and three other individuals in federal district court in Boston, seeking $120 million in damages; the U.S. Attorney had considered a criminal indictment but concluded the evidence fell short of the standard of proof for criminality.
facts.quote: In September, the U.S. Department of Justice filed suit in federal district court in Boston, seeking $120 million in damages from Harvard University, one tenured professor, and three other individuals. The U.S. attorney also considered a criminal indictment, but concluded that the evidence fell short of standards of proof for criminality.

facts.claim: On June 28, 2004, Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) ruled on summary judgment that the USAID Cooperative Agreements were valid contracts between Harvard and USAID that created an obligation to remain free of conflicts of interest, and that actions by Hay and Shleifer breached that duty. The court described the project as a government-sponsored Harvard effort to assist Russia in developing capital markets and foreign investments.
facts.quote: the Cooperative Agreements were valid contracts between Harvard and USAID, that they created an obligation to remain free of conflicts of interest, and that actions by Hay and Shleifer breached that duty. [...] alleged improprieties in a government-sponsored Harvard project to assist Russia in developing capital markets and foreign investments.

facts.claim: The 2004 ruling found Harvard had violated its USAID contract by certifying that the Russia program met contractual requirements while the two men were making investments, but cleared the University of knowingly defrauding the government and so of treble damages. The judge found Shleifer liable on one of five charges (conspiracy to help Hay commit fraud) and Hay liable for two counts of fraud and one of conspiracy, and held that the men were acting for individual benefit, not within the scope of their Harvard employment.
facts.quote: Judge Woodlock found that Harvard did violate the USAID contract by certifying that the Russian program was fulfilling contractual requirements even while the two men were making the investments. But the court cleared the University of knowingly defrauding the government, and hence of liability for treble damages. [...] the judge did find Shleifer liable on one of five charges: that of conspiracy to help Hay commit fraud. He found Hay liable for two counts of fraud and one of conspiracy.

facts.claim: In August 2005 the case settled: Harvard agreed to pay $26.5 million, Shleifer $2 million, and Hay between $500,000 and $2 million depending on his income over the next 10 years; a firm owned by Shleifer's wife had already paid $1.5 million. Shleifer was debarred from USAID work for two years and Hay for five. None of the defendants admitted liability. The Justice Department described the total as more than $31 million; USAID's outlay on the project had been about $40 million on a $57 million contract.
facts.quote: Harvard would pay $26.5 million to settle the $120-million civil suit. [...] Shleifer agreed to pay $2 million to the government; Hay's portion of the settlement will fall between $500,000 and $2 million, depending on his income in the next 10 years. [...] Shleifer has also been disbarred from USAID work for two years, and Hay for five. [...] none of the defendants admitted liability for wrongdoing.

openQuestions: No source opened this session states that HIID or its advisers designed the 1995 loans-for-shares auctions or Russia's 1992-94 voucher auctions; the sources describe HIID as advising Chubais's GKI on privatization and, under later agreements, on capital-market and legal reform. See the claims entry appended to research/handoffs/russia-loans-for-shares.json.
The Crimson (2005-08-05) says Shleifer and Hay agreed to a two-year USAID debarment; Harvard Magazine (2005-11) says two years for Shleifer and five for Hay. Check the settlement agreement.
Hay's settlement share is reported as $500,000-$2 million (Harvard Magazine) and $1-2 million (Institutional Investor), depending on future income.
The Russian Privatization Center (an HIID-linked body often cited in this context) could not be sourced this session; the search budget ran out before a primary source was found.

A DOJ/U.S. Attorney (D. Mass.) press release on the 2005 settlement was not located in the justice.gov search results; the $31 million-plus total is from Harvard Magazine's and Institutional Investor's accounts of the DOJ statement.
